rv.q: Icke, best known for his radical Shakespeares and startlingly reworked classics, here brilliantly re-examines the recent past at a time when we’re arguably more surveilled, monitored, and eavesdropped-upon than ever.
It makes a story safely stowed in the past feel live and speak to a present in which truth, narrative control, abuse of power and artistic integrity are all scarily back in the spotlight.

So it's fitting that Robert Icke 's ingenious staging of the 2006. German espionage thriller The Lives of Others feels like a vast act of transfiguration – turning grimy state machinery into heartstopping visual poetry.
And the achievement of the production, played without interval and often using a stage revolve to create a sense of remorseless scrutiny, is that it has its own strange, nightmarish logic.
As it is, it's not prime Icke, but he's at least done a fine job in turning a 20-year-old foreign language film into gripping West End entertainment.

And though the deliberate, thematically appropriate distancing effect keeps us from ever truly connecting with the characters, the piece remains a compelling study of paranoia and the fragility of human connection.

As the adaptor and director, he imposes his aesthetic on every aspect of the evening — as he did in his recent update of Oedipus — but in the end you are often left admiring the bravura flourishes rather than being drawn into the story itself.
But to me, this does not manage the immensely difficult task it sets itself.
His vision is an immense achievement not least because it is nigh-on perfect in execution.
This is a gripping and totally absorbing night out, with star casting that pays off in spades.
The director/designer pairing is infused with an innate mutual understanding and their execution here is a finely orchestrated gem.
Icke’s production, in itself, makes a persuasive case for that vital contribution.
The blend of menace and absurdity makes for an absorbing spectacle.
This production seems like a match made in dystopian heaven.
While this production does not reach such heights, it remains a solid, entertaining, and suspenseful two hours.
The pacing in this play was too slow for my liking, unhelped by an irritating habit to ‘show’ as well as ‘tell’.
There are too many ideas onstage here for comfort, and certainly too many for clarity and impact.
Combining psychological tension, exceptional performances and visually arresting stagecraft, it is a truly unmissable piece of theatre that keeps its audience gripped from start to finish.
Stephen Dillane is superb as Wiesler.
Icke has created an exhilarating piece of theatre.
A must watch in the West End this year!

But Icke has vision like few other theatre directors and his production hums with an ominous energy, capturing the terrifying menace of Stasi East Germany and the brightness of the lights extinguished too soon during those bleak years.
The result is a slick and stylish production that acts as a breath of fresh air in the West End and shows exactly how adapting a movie for the stage can be done with such finesse.
Robert Icke has created a very slick production, with some inventive staging and strong visuals.
This is an accomplished and compelling adaptation by Robert Icke (Oedipus, Oresteia, Romeo & Juliet).
What struck me most was the production's remarkably cinematic quality.

The serious tone of the play and the supposed political acumen, however, are undermined by the somewhat unlikely innocence of Dreyman and the ridiculous idea that Hempf would play out his secret affair in a flat he knows to be under full surveillance.
I thought it was an absolutely superb production, a fantastic adaptation of a really good film, and I'm giving it a big fat five stars ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️.
The Lives of Others takes the tension and intimacy of a cinematic spy thriller and finds an extraordinarily effective way to realise it on stage.
Fittingly for a surveillance drama, this is a must watch.

cn.t: Robert Icke's slick, technically impressive adaptation of the Oscar-winning film divides critics. While most praise the staging, design, and strong performances (especially Dillane), some find it emotionally cold and overly stylized compared to the film's subtlety.
